reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When building models that make binary choices, we often need to convert any continuous measurement into a probability between zero and one. Linear functions fail here because they grow without bound as inputs get large. We need a smooth curve that maps the entire real number line into a bounded interval.

Pierre François Verhulst faced a similar problem when modeling population growth, leading him to the logistic function. By dividing one by the sum of one and an exponential term, the output naturally stays strictly between zero and one for any finite input. As the input grows very large or very negative, the exponential term dominates in a way that clamps the result smoothly at the boundaries.

Exploring this curve reveals how its parameters control its behavior. The steepness parameter adjusts how quickly the transition happens, while the midpoint shifts the center of the curve along the horizontal axis. Together, they create a versatile mapping tool used across mathematics and machine learning.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic function $y = 1 / (1 + exp(-k * (x - x0)))$ maps any real input smoothly into the interval from zero to one.
reply.instructions: Adjust the steepness, midpoint, and marker position to observe how the logistic curve and its slope change across different inputs.
